questions.prompt: What does the chapter mean by discovering power?
choices: Finding the hidden leverage or asymmetry that changes what a move is worth
Collecting more resources than the other side
Choosing the most inspiring slogan before acting

explanation.gentle: The chapter treats power as leverage inside the situation, not as visible strength alone.
explanation.direct: Discovering power means finding the asymmetry or structure that changes the contest.
explanation.competitive: It is about the bend in the field, not the size of the pile.

questions.prompt: Why does David and Goliath work here as a strategy example rather than only a courage example?
choices: Because David secretly had more physical strength
Because the fight changed once David refused the close contest that favored Goliath
Because the chapter says courage always beats armor

explanation.gentle: The lesson is about changed terms. David's move matters because the contest stops rewarding Goliath's strongest advantages.
explanation.direct: Distance and mobility alter the structure of the fight.
explanation.competitive: David wins by rejecting the giant's game.

questions.prompt: What is the chapter's warning about copying best practices from a winner?
choices: Visible practices may be only the surface expression of a deeper system advantage
Best practices are useless unless the team is already the market leader
Imitation works only in personal rather than business settings

explanation.gentle: The chapter warns that copying what can be seen first may miss the architecture carrying the result.
explanation.direct: Surface imitation underperforms when the reinforcing system stays with the original player.
explanation.competitive: Stealing the shell leaves the engine behind.

questions.prompt: Tessa's campus paper cannot match a larger outlet on total volume. What response fits the chapter best?
choices: Work longer hours until the team matches the larger outlet article for article
Shift the contest toward a narrow, fast lane where the larger outlet responds more slowly
Pause publication until the paper has equal staffing

explanation.gentle: The chapter favors changed terms over head-on matching when an asymmetry is available.
explanation.direct: Tessa gains leverage by moving the competition into a lane her team can own.
explanation.competitive: She stops losing the wrong race and starts owning the right one.

questions.prompt: What is Wal-Mart mainly showing in this chapter?
choices: That low prices alone explain strategic power
That one strong local manager matters more than any system
That a reinforcing network can carry power more deeply than one visible outlet can

explanation.gentle: Wal-Mart's lesson here is structural power, not one isolated visible habit.
explanation.direct: The network underneath the stores is the deeper advantage.
explanation.competitive: The engine is the point, not the storefront.

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures asymmetric-cost competition?
choices: Winning by making the opponent's responses more expensive to sustain than your own
Winning only by using lower prices in every market
Winning through secrecy even when the contest terms never change

explanation.gentle: The chapter uses Marshall and Roche to show a contest shaped around unequal burden.
explanation.direct: Asymmetric cost means the race hurts the other side more to keep running.
explanation.competitive: You bend the race so their miles cost more.

questions.prompt: Ben and Clara keep arguing about being disorganized until they identify one repeating schedule choke point. Why does that fit the chapter?
choices: Because hidden leverage can sit in one constraint that governs a much larger pattern
Because personal life has no real strategic structure
Because any narrow fix is always more important than the wider system

explanation.gentle: The chapter's logic applies because one redesigned pressure point can change the value of many later moves.
explanation.direct: A hidden constraint can carry more power than a general promise to try harder.
explanation.competitive: They found the bend instead of lecturing themselves again.

questions.prompt: What is the strongest sign that a move is only a clever trick and not durable leverage?
choices: It surprises the opponent once but does not keep changing later moves
It makes the opponent adapt at a higher cost
It grows stronger as system reinforcement builds around it

explanation.gentle: The chapter keeps this limit visible so novelty is not confused with lasting power.
explanation.direct: Durable leverage continues to alter the contest after surprise fades.
explanation.competitive: If the edge dies after one hit, it was never the engine.

questions.prompt: Why can a smaller player still matter more strategically than a larger rival?
choices: Because size usually stops mattering once a contest begins
Because leverage can change which variables the contest actually rewards
Because larger rivals always become complacent

explanation.gentle: The chapter does not erase size. It shows that leverage can make a different variable matter more.
explanation.direct: A smaller actor can become stronger strategically by shifting the contest onto better terms.
explanation.competitive: The bend can make the small player hit above its weight.

questions.prompt: How does this chapter prepare the reader for a chapter on bad strategy?
choices: By showing that bad strategy is often vague about values but still good at leverage
By showing that one failure mode of bad strategy is never discovering or using the leverage already in the situation
By arguing that bad strategy happens only when leaders have too little information

explanation.gentle: Once leverage becomes visible, it is easier to see how a plan can fail by staying blind to it.
explanation.direct: The next chapter can define bad strategy more sharply because missing hidden power is one of its clearest failures.
explanation.competitive: Bad strategy keeps fighting on bad terms even when the bend is right there.
